The Red Tour was the third headlining concert tour by American singer-songwriter [Taylor Swift](/page/Taylor_Swift), undertaken in support of her fourth studio album, [Red](/page/Red) (2012).[[1]](#ref-1) It commenced on March 13, 2013, at the CenturyLink Center in [Omaha, Nebraska](/page/Omaha,_Nebraska), and concluded on June 12, 2014, at the Singapore Indoor Stadium in [Singapore](/page/Singapore), encompassing 86 performances across 12 countries on four continents.[[2]](#ref-2) The tour featured elaborate stage production with thematic elements inspired by the album's scarlet motif, including dynamic lighting, video projections, and a catwalk extending into the audience, while Swift performed a setlist blending tracks from Red with selections from her earlier [discography](/page/Discography).[[3]](#ref-3) Guest performers such as [Ed Sheeran](/page/Ed_Sheeran) joined for select dates, contributing to collaborations like "[Everything Has Changed](/page/Everything_Has_Changed)."[[1]](#ref-1)
The tour's initial leg consisted of 66 arena and stadium shows across [North America](/page/North_America), with tickets going on sale in November 2012 and rapid sell-outs reported for many venues.[[4]](#ref-4) Subsequent extensions included dates in [Europe](/page/Europe), [Asia](/page/Asia), and [Oceania](/page/Oceania), transforming it into a global production that played to over 1.7 million attendees.[[2]](#ref-2) Critically, the shows were praised for Swift's vocal maturity, engaging [storytelling](/page/Storytelling), and high-energy [choreography](/page/Choreography), solidifying her transition from [country](/page/Country) roots toward pop superstardom.[[5]](#ref-5) Commercially, it achieved unprecedented success for a [country](/page/Country) artist, grossing $150.2 million in revenue and setting a record as the highest-earning tour in the genre until surpassed by later efforts.[[2]](#ref-2)

## Background

### Album Promotion Context

Taylor Swift released her fourth studio album, [Red](/page/Red), on October 22, 2012, through [Big Machine Records](/page/Big_Machine_Records).[[6]](#ref-6) The album marked a significant evolution in her sound, incorporating stronger pop influences alongside her established country roots, as evidenced by collaborations with producers like [Max Martin](/page/Max_Martin) and Shellback who brought electronic and rock elements into tracks such as "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together."[[7]](#ref-7)
Red achieved immediate commercial success, debuting at number one on the Billboard 200 with 1.21 million copies sold in its first week in the United States, the highest sales week for an album by a female artist since 2002.[[8]](#ref-8) The album's themes centered on love, heartbreak, and emotional maturity, drawing from Swift's personal experiences with failed relationships and growth, which provided a more introspective lens compared to her earlier work.[[9]](#ref-9)
Initial promotional efforts for [Red](/page/Red) included the release of lead single "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" on August 13, 2012, which topped the [Billboard Hot 100](/page/Billboard_Hot_100) and introduced the album's pop-leaning direction through television performances and [music videos](/page/Dave_Meyers_videography).[[8]](#ref-8) Follow-up single "[I Knew You Were Trouble](/page/I_Knew_You_Were_Trouble)," released on October 9, 2012, further amplified promotion with its dubstep-infused production, peaking at number two on the Hot 100 and tying directly into the album's [narrative](/page/Narrative) of turbulent romance.
To build on this momentum, Swift announced The Red Tour on October 25, 2012, just days after the album's release, positioning it as her third headlining concert effort following the [Fearless Tour](/page/Fearless_Tour) (2009–2010) and [Speak Now World Tour](/page/Speak_Now_World_Tour) (2011–2012).[[10]](#ref-10) This arena-scale tour was conceived as a direct extension of [Red](/page/Red)'s marketing strategy, aiming to showcase the album's songs live while leveraging its thematic depth to engage fans through storytelling performances.[[11]](#ref-11)

### Tour Announcement and Initial Planning

The Red Tour was officially announced by [Taylor Swift](/page/Taylor_Swift) on October 25, 2012, during promotional activities tied to her album Red, with the initial North American leg comprising 45 dates across arenas and stadiums, set to commence on March 13, 2013, at the CenturyLink Center in [Omaha, Nebraska](/page/Omaha,_Nebraska).[[12]](#ref-12)[[11]](#ref-11) Early planning for the tour had begun in the summer of 2012, focusing on logistics for a large-scale production to support the album's themes of emotional intensity and relationships.[[4]](#ref-4)
Opening acts for the U.S. leg were selected during this initial phase, including British singer-songwriter [Ed Sheeran](/page/Ed_Sheeran), who collaborated with Swift on the album track "[Everything Has Changed](/page/Everything_Has_Changed)" and was announced as the primary support for all North American dates; rising pop artist [Austin Mahone](/page/Austin_Mahone), added for select stadium performances.[[13]](#ref-13)[[14]](#ref-14)
Due to overwhelming presale demand following the November 16, 2012, ticket release—where multiple shows, including those at [Los Angeles](/page/Los_Angeles)' Staples Center and New York's [Madison Square Garden](/page/Madison_Square_Garden), sold out in under a minute—additional dates were rapidly added, expanding the North American leg to 58 shows by December 2012 while maintaining accessibility with tickets priced under $50 at every venue.[[15]](#ref-15)[[11]](#ref-11)
In 2013, as the North American dates progressed successfully, Swift announced international expansions, including an Oceania leg in late 2013 in [Australia](/page/Australia) and [New Zealand](/page/New_Zealand), a European leg starting February 2014 in [London](/page/London), [England](/page/England), and an Asian leg starting June 2014 in [Jakarta](/page/Jakarta), [Indonesia](/page/Indonesia), ultimately extending the tour to 86 shows across 12 countries and concluding on June 12, 2014, at the [Singapore Indoor Stadium](/page/Singapore_Indoor_Stadium).[[16]](#ref-16)[[17]](#ref-17)[[18]](#ref-18)[[19]](#ref-19)

## Production

### Stage Design and Technical Elements

The stage design for The Red Tour was crafted by Taylor Swift's [production team](/page/Production_team) to capture the album's themes of emotional maturity and urban sophistication, incorporating a central catwalk that extended into the audience for intimate interactions, elevated platforms on a double-storey structure, and thematic backdrops such as a rotating wind-up carousel during "Mean" and a New York cityscape projection for "22."[[20]](#ref-20)[[21]](#ref-21) These elements allowed for fluid transitions across the 18-song set, with the red color scheme dominating props and settings to reinforce the tour's aesthetic. Rehearsals focused on seamless integration of these features, ensuring smooth shifts between high-energy segments and acoustic moments on the rear B-stage platform.[[22]](#ref-22)
The tour's audio setup prioritized arena-wide clarity for Swift's blend of pop and country influences, utilizing a [d&b audiotechnik](/page/D&b_audiotechnik) line-array speaker system that included 24 J Series mains, 24 J Series side hangs, 10 V Series 270° hangs, and multiple [subwoofer](/page/Subwoofer) configurations for robust low-end response.[[23]](#ref-23) All performers, including Swift and her seven-member band, relied on in-ear monitors via 24 [Shure](/page/Shure) PSM-1000 wireless systems, with mixes customized by monitor engineer Jordan Kolenc to handle dynamic vocal and instrumental shifts.[[23]](#ref-23) This collaboration with audio engineers like front-of-house mixer David Payne enabled precise control, using three [DiGiCo](/page/DiGiCo) SD7 consoles linked at 96 kHz for 96 input channels across the production.[[23]](#ref-23)
Lighting and visual elements enhanced the thematic immersion, with a extensive rig of moving head fixtures and LED screens delivering dynamic red motifs synchronized to songs like "Red," alongside video projections that depicted urban skylines and narrative scenes.[[24]](#ref-24) Pyrotechnics added intensity to high-energy tracks such as "I Knew You Were Trouble," featuring sparks and flames integrated into the drumline sequences.[[25]](#ref-25) Confetti cannons, often launching red and multicolored pieces, punctuated celebratory moments like the finale "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together," with gold fireworks exploding overhead to close shows.[[25]](#ref-25) These technical components were rigorously tested in rehearsals to maintain synchronization throughout the performance.[[26]](#ref-26)

### Wardrobe and Visual Aesthetics

The wardrobe for Taylor Swift's Red Tour was primarily designed by Emmy-winning [costume designer](/page/Costume_designer) Marina Toybina, who created custom pieces inspired by the singer's songs to reflect themes of passion, art, and individuality.[[27]](#ref-27)[[28]](#ref-28) Toybina collaborated closely with Swift on the [set list](/page/Set_list), [choreography](/page/Choreography), and staging concepts, resulting in numerous costume changes per show—reportedly up to 11—that emphasized a bold, glamorous [evolution](/page/Evolution) from Swift's country roots toward pop aesthetics.[[28]](#ref-28) These outfits often featured red accents and sparkly elements, such as a [gold](/page/Gold) sequined top paired with black shorts for high-energy openers, symbolizing the album's fiery emotional intensity.[[29]](#ref-29)
Thematic progression in the wardrobe mirrored the set list's narrative arc, with edgy, rock-infused looks like black leather shorts, a lace blouse, [fedora](/page/Fedora), and red Oxfords kicking off the show for tracks like "State of Grace," evoking urban grit and rebellion.[[29]](#ref-29)[[28]](#ref-28) In contrast, ballads such as "Love Story" showcased elegant red gowns with opera gloves and matching shoes, blending fairy-tale romance with dramatic stage presence to highlight Swift's storytelling versatility.[[29]](#ref-29) Other variations included striped tops with red pants for playful segments and a circus ringleader ensemble complete with [tailcoat](/page/Tailcoat) and boots for upbeat numbers, ensuring visual dynamism across the two-hour performance.[[29]](#ref-29)
Accessories played a key role in enhancing the looks' cohesion and fan appeal, incorporating items like custom fedoras, sparkly Oxfords, and subtle jewelry that balanced aspirational glamour with relatable everyday elements, such as heart-printed T-shirts paired with shorts.[[29]](#ref-29) These choices fostered audience connection by echoing the album's themes of youthful heartbreak and empowerment in accessible yet elevated styles. Behind the scenes, Toybina's team conducted extensive fittings and alterations during rehearsals, focusing on fabric selection, draping, and handcrafting to guarantee mobility for dance routines and quick changes amid the tour's intricate staging.[[28]](#ref-28) This preparation, spanning over three weeks of sketching and sewing, allowed seamless transitions that synchronized with lighting cues for immersive visual impact.[[28]](#ref-28)

### Sponsors and Partnerships

The Red Tour benefited from several key sponsorships that provided financial support and enhanced promotional opportunities, with [Diet Coke](/page/Diet_Coke) emerging as a primary partner through a long-term agreement announced in January 2013. This collaboration centered on [Diet Coke](/page/Diet_Coke)'s "Stay Extraordinary" platform, aligning the brand with Swift's image of empowerment and uniqueness, and included integrated marketing activations tied to the tour's themes.[[30]](#ref-30)
Elizabeth Arden served as another major sponsor, leveraging its fragrance licensing deal with Swift—encompassing scents like Wonderstruck—to create branded experiences that connected the tour to beauty and personal style. The partnership focused on VIP elements, such as exclusive access and promotional displays that highlighted Swift's endorsement role, helping to drive fragrance sales among fans during the tour's rollout.[[31]](#ref-31)
Keds acted as the official footwear sponsor for the North American leg, releasing limited-edition Champion sneakers inspired by the Red album aesthetic and distributing them through tour-related merchandise channels. This deal extended to fan engagement initiatives, including on-site styling activations and contests offering prizes like backstage passes and seat upgrades, which were promoted starting in March 2013 as part of the tour's initial planning.[[32]](#ref-32)[[33]](#ref-33)
Regional partnerships further expanded the tour's commercial reach, particularly in [Asia](/page/Asia). Cornetto, an ice cream brand under [Unilever](/page/Unilever), launched a "Red" flavored product exclusively for the Asian leg in 2014, featuring Swift's imagery in packaging and advertisements to capitalize on the tour's momentum. Similarly, [Toyota](/page/Toyota) became the official automotive sponsor for [Southeast Asia](/page/Southeast_Asia), tying its involvement to a road safety campaign across five countries and providing branded vehicles for tour logistics.[[34]](#ref-34)[[35]](#ref-35)
These sponsorships collectively generated additional revenue through merchandise collaborations, such as the [Keds](/page/Keds) sneakers and [Elizabeth Arden](/page/Elizabeth_Arden) fragrance bundles available at venues, while sponsor-backed contests for meet-and-greets amplified fan interaction and brand visibility from the announcement phase onward.[[31]](#ref-31)

## Concert Details

### Performance Synopsis

The Red Tour concerts typically ran for approximately two hours, divided into distinct acts that traced an emotional arc from high-energy exuberance to intimate reflection and triumphant closure.[[36]](#ref-36) The opening act burst with vibrant performances of tracks from the Red album, featuring explosive choreography, dynamic lighting, and elaborate stage visuals to immerse audiences in themes of passion and turmoil.[[37]](#ref-37)[[38]](#ref-38)
A mid-show acoustic segment transitioned to a secondary stage, where Swift delivered stripped-down renditions emphasizing vulnerability and connection, allowing for seamless flow between high-production spectacle and personal storytelling. This portion highlighted the tour's use of multiple platforms, including catwalks extending into the crowd, to bridge the gap between performer and audience in large arenas.[[37]](#ref-37)[[39]](#ref-39)
The finale escalated with career-spanning hits, building to an electrifying peak that unified the crowd in shared celebration. Audience interaction wove throughout.[[37]](#ref-37)
Theatrical elements enriched the narrative, such as a circus-inspired interlude with dancers and aerialists during "The Lucky One," where movement and visuals underscored themes of fame and fleeting luck through stylized storytelling.[[39]](#ref-39)[[40]](#ref-40)
Regional adaptations tailored the experience, with cultural nods like extended encores in Asian dates and locale-specific gestures—such as a Union Jack T-shirt in London—to resonate with international crowds.[[37]](#ref-37)[[41]](#ref-41)

### Set List and Variations

The core setlist for The Red Tour's debut performance on March 13, 2013, at the CenturyLink Center in Omaha, Nebraska, consisted of 18 songs drawn primarily from the Red album, interspersed with selections from Swift's earlier catalog to showcase her evolving sound. The show opened with high-energy rock-infused tracks like "State of Grace" and "Holy Ground," transitioned to pop-country hybrids such as "Red" and "You Belong With Me" (performed in a 1960s remix style), and included fan favorites like "Mean" and "22." Mid-show highlights featured collaborations and emotional peaks, including "Everything Has Changed" with Ed Sheeran, "I Knew You Were Trouble," "All Too Well," "Love Story," and "Treacherous," before closing with "Long Live" and an encore of "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together." This structure emphasized the album's thematic blend of heartbreak and resilience, with Swift playing guitar and piano throughout.[[42]](#ref-42)
A key element of unpredictability was the acoustic "surprise song" segment, performed on a rising B-stage platform, where Swift selected tracks from her discography based on fan requests gathered via social media. These solo or minimally accompanied renditions, often on guitar or piano, varied nightly to foster intimacy and replay value; examples included "Sad Beautiful Tragic" in early North American shows and covers or variants like an acoustic "Red" to tie back to the tour's theme. In Europe and later legs, this slot sometimes rotated to include "Begin Again" for pacing, while Australia dates featured a fixed acoustic "You Belong With Me" without a full surprise element due to scheduling. This tradition, which became a staple in Swift's live performances, highlighted her catalog depth and direct engagement with audiences.[[3]](#ref-3)
The setlist evolved modestly over the tour's 86 dates to accommodate regional preferences, time constraints, and production adjustments, maintaining about 80% consistency while allowing for freshness.[[41]](#ref-41) For instance, "Stay Stay Stay" (with Lumineers' "Ho Hey" excerpts) was temporarily removed after July 2013 for brevity but reinstated briefly, and "Everything Has Changed" was dropped post-North America to streamline the European leg. Additions like "Begin Again" appeared in select European and Oceanic shows to emphasize country roots. A representative full setlist from the March 28, 2013, show at Prudential Center in Newark, New Jersey, illustrates this: it opened with "State of Grace," followed by "Holy Ground," "Red," "You Belong With Me," "The Lucky One," "Mean," "Stay Stay Stay," "22," "The Story of Us," "I Knew You Were Trouble," "Everything Has Changed" (with Ed Sheeran), "Treacherous," "The Last Time," "All Too Well," "Love Story," then acoustic "Sad Beautiful Tragic," "Long Live," and encore "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together," acoustic "Red." These tweaks ensured dynamic pacing without overhauling the musical core.[[3]](#ref-3)[[43]](#ref-43)
Instrumentation supported the tour's genre fusion, with Swift's seven-member live band—The Agency—featuring a [pianist](/page/Pianist), two guitarists, violinist/fiddler Caitlin Evanson for country-inflected tracks like "Mean" and "Treacherous," a bass guitarist, multi-instrumentalist, and drummer to handle electronic beats and synth elements in pop numbers such as "22" and "I Knew You Were Trouble." Evanson's fiddle added twang to acoustic segments, while electronic production via [DiGiCo](/page/DiGiCo) consoles enhanced the arena-scale energy for remixed hits. This setup allowed seamless shifts between organic folk-country arrangements and polished electronic pop, underscoring Red's stylistic breadth.[[44]](#ref-44)[[23]](#ref-23)[[45]](#ref-45)

## Commercial Performance

### Ticket Sales

Ticket sales for The Red Tour began with exclusive presales on November 11, 2012, targeted at American Express cardmembers and members of Taylor Swift's official fan club, providing early access to select dates across the North American leg.[[46]](#ref-46) The general public onsale commenced on November 16, 2012, via Ticketmaster, and the overwhelming demand resulted in rapid sell-outs for most announced shows, often within minutes of tickets becoming available.[[12]](#ref-12)[[47]](#ref-47) This initial surge necessitated the addition of extra dates in cities such as Los Angeles, Philadelphia, and Foxborough to meet fan interest.[[15]](#ref-15)
Pricing for standard seats was structured to promote accessibility, ranging from $39.50 to $109.50 depending on the venue and seating section, with Swift specifically requesting that each of the 59 shows include tickets priced under $50.[[48]](#ref-48)[[12]](#ref-12) Premium VIP packages offered enhanced experiences, priced up to $389 and including elements such as top-tier reserved floor seating in the first 20 rows, a meet-and-greet opportunity, an autographed copy of the Red album, and a commemorative laminate.[[49]](#ref-49)[[50]](#ref-50) Fixed pricing prevailed in the primary market, as dynamic pricing models had not yet become common in the industry.
The presale mechanics effectively highlighted the tour's strong fan demand, exemplified by venues like Toronto's [Rogers Centre](/page/Rogers_Centre) selling out in five minutes and Detroit's [Ford Field](/page/Ford_Field) in ten minutes during the initial onsale window.[[51]](#ref-51) American Express's involvement extended sponsor perks, granting cardmembers priority VIP access to foster exclusive fan engagement.[[52]](#ref-52) Challenges arose from the intense interest, including reports of [scalping](/page/Scalping) on secondary markets where resale prices escalated rapidly, though primary sales channels focused on fan club verification to prioritize authentic purchasers over bots and resellers.[[53]](#ref-53)

### Box Office Revenue and Records

The Red Tour achieved significant financial success, grossing a total of $150.2 million across 86 shows attended by 1.7 million fans, with an average revenue of $1.7 million per night.[[2]](#ref-2) This performance marked it as the highest-grossing tour by a [country](/page/Country) artist at the time, eclipsing the previous record set by [Faith Hill](/page/Faith_Hill) and Tim McGraw's [Soul2Soul II Tour](/page/Soul2Soul_II_Tour), which earned $141 million over its run.[[2]](#ref-2) The tour's strong [box office](/page/Box_office) results were bolstered by rapid sell-outs, reflecting high demand that drove consistent per-show earnings.[[54]](#ref-54)
Revenue was primarily generated from its North American leg, which alone accounted for over two-thirds of the total, though the international portions in [Europe](/page/Europe), [Oceania](/page/Oceania), and [Asia](/page/Asia) added substantial contributions through stadium performances.[[2]](#ref-2) Standout shows highlighted the tour's scale, such as the two-night stand at [Gillette Stadium](/page/Gillette_Stadium) in [Foxborough, Massachusetts](/page/Foxborough,_Massachusetts), which drew 110,712 attendees and grossed $9.4 million.[[2]](#ref-2) Another notable performance was the single show at Heinz Field in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, attracting 56,047 fans for $4.7 million in revenue.[[2]](#ref-2)
In Pollstar's year-end rankings for 2013, the tour placed #1 among North American tours with $112.7 million grossed that year and #8 worldwide with $131 million, underscoring its dominance despite spanning into 2014.[[54]](#ref-54)[[55]](#ref-55) These figures established The Red Tour as a benchmark for [country music](/page/Country_music) concert economics, demonstrating Taylor Swift's ability to command premium ticket prices and large-scale venues globally.[[2]](#ref-2)

## Reception

### Critical Reviews

Critics widely praised Taylor Swift's vocal maturation and commanding stage presence during The Red Tour, highlighting her artistic evolution from country roots to polished pop artistry. Rolling Stone praised Swift as a master at connecting with her audience, noting that her amps go up to 22 during the performance heavily drawn from the Red album.[[56]](#ref-56) Similarly, The Guardian commended her transformation of tracks like "All Too Well" into wrenching ballads, showcasing vocal depth and a shift from "country ingenue" to slick pop entertainer, all while maintaining a staggeringly nice and engaging demeanor.[[37]](#ref-37)
Feedback on the tour's production was mixed, with outlets lauding its grand scale while occasionally critiquing its reliance on effects that sometimes overshadowed vocal nuances. Billboard described the show as bringing [Red](/page/Red) vividly to life through immersive spectacle, including elaborate staging and crowd interaction that left audiences awestruck.[[3]](#ref-3) In contrast, The Boston Globe observed that despite on-pitch delivery, Swift's reedy voice struggled at times amid the fireworks, rising drummers, and costume changes, suggesting the production's intensity occasionally masked inconsistencies.[[57]](#ref-57) The Los Angeles Times likened the overall setup to a "touring [Cirque du Soleil](/page/Cirque_du_Soleil)," praising its smooth choreography and high-energy transitions but noting a scripted feel with limited spontaneity.[[58]](#ref-58)
International reception emphasized Swift's ability to foster deep fan connections and broaden her appeal across cultures. In the UK, The Guardian highlighted the intense devotion of the 15,000-strong [O2 Arena](/page/The_O2_Arena) crowd, with Swift's personal anecdotes and [Union Jack](/page/Union_Jack) gestures amplifying emotional bonds.[[37]](#ref-37) Australian reviews, such as from [the Sydney Morning Herald](/page/The_Sydney_Morning_Herald), underscored the tour's crossover success, praising its blend of polished spectacle and heartfelt moments like stripped-back renditions of "[All Too Well](/page/All_Too_Well)," which resonated universally with 47,000 fans at Etihad Stadium and demonstrated genre-blending poise.[[59]](#ref-59)
Aggregate scores from major publications averaged around 4 out of 5 stars, with recurring themes of strong emotional connectivity amid challenges in seamlessly integrating country and pop elements. Outlets like [Rolling Stone](/page/Rolling_Stone) and [The Guardian](/page/The_Guardian) frequently awarded high marks for Swift's relatability and showmanship, though some noted the genre shifts occasionally felt disjointed in live execution.[[56]](#ref-56)[[37]](#ref-37)

### Fan and Industry Accolades

The Red Tour garnered substantial acclaim from fans and industry professionals, affirming its status as a landmark production in Taylor Swift's career. At the 2013 [Billboard](/page/Billboard) Touring Awards, the tour secured the Top Package Award, recognizing it as the highest-grossing concert run featuring three or more artists on the bill.[[60]](#ref-60) It also ranked seventh overall on [Billboard](/page/Billboard)'s year-end [list](/page/List_of_denim_jeans_brands) of the top 25 tours of 2013, reflecting its broad commercial and artistic resonance.[[61]](#ref-61) Furthermore, the tour earned a nomination for the fan-voted Eventful Fans' Choice Award at the same event, highlighting Swift's dedicated supporter base.[[62]](#ref-62)
Fan enthusiasm translated into notable nods across major awards ceremonies, emphasizing the tour's appeal to younger audiences. The production was nominated for Choice Summer Tour at the 2013 [Teen Choice Awards](/page/Teen_Choice_Awards), a category determined by public voting, where it competed against high-profile acts like One Direction's Take Me Home Tour.[[63]](#ref-63) These recognitions underscored the tour's vibrant energy and Swift's ability to connect with fans through elaborate staging and personal performances.
Industry accolades further cemented the tour's influence, particularly within [country music](/page/Country_music) circles. [Pollstar](/page/Pollstar) named the Red Tour the top-grossing concert run in [North America](/page/North_America) for 2013, positioning it as a pivotal breakthrough for female [country](/page/Country) artists by surpassing previous benchmarks for the [genre](/page/Genre).[[54]](#ref-54) In 2015, Swift received the 50th Anniversary Milestone Award at the 50th [Academy of Country Music Awards](/page/Academy_of_Country_Music_Awards), recognizing her as the youngest Entertainer of the Year winner in ACM history.[[64]](#ref-64)

## Tour Execution

### Schedule and Locations

The Red Tour's itinerary encompassed four legs over 15 months, commencing on March 13, 2013, at the CenturyLink Center in [Omaha, Nebraska](/page/Omaha,_Nebraska), and concluding on June 12, 2014, at the [Singapore Indoor Stadium](/page/Singapore_Indoor_Stadium) in [Singapore](/page/Singapore). Spanning 12 countries across [North America](/page/North_America), [Oceania](/page/Oceania), [Europe](/page/Europe), and [Asia](/page/Asia), the tour featured 86 performances in arenas and stadiums with capacities typically between 20,000 and 50,000, though select high-demand markets utilized larger stadium venues for multiple nights. Overall, it drew more than 1.7 million attendees, averaging approximately 20,000 per show, with logistical coordination involving extensive intercontinental travel to accommodate the global scope.[[65]](#ref-65)[[66]](#ref-66)[[67]](#ref-67)
The North American leg formed the tour's core, comprising 66 shows from March 13 to September 21, 2013, across 29 U.S. states and three Canadian provinces ([Ontario](/page/Ontario), [Manitoba](/page/Manitoba), and [British Columbia](/page/British_Columbia)). Performances took place in a mix of arenas, such as [TD Garden](/page/TD_Garden) in [Boston](/page/Boston) and [Scotiabank](/page/Scotiabank) Place in [Ottawa](/page/Ottawa), and stadiums including Cowboys Stadium in [Arlington, Texas](/page/Arlington,_Texas), and [MetLife Stadium](/page/MetLife_Stadium) in [East Rutherford, New Jersey](/page/East_Rutherford,_New_Jersey). This segment highlighted Swift's strong domestic fanbase, with consistent sellouts in mid-sized venues averaging 20,000 to 25,000 attendees per night.[[68]](#ref-68)[[67]](#ref-67)[[1]](#ref-1)

### Opening Acts and Special Guests

The Red Tour featured a rotating lineup of opening acts tailored to regional markets, with [Ed Sheeran](/page/Ed_Sheeran) serving as the primary opener for all North American and European dates, performing a 30- to 45-minute set that highlighted his acoustic [folk-pop](/page/Folk-pop) style to complement Swift's evolving sound.[[1]](#ref-1) Additional North American openers included emerging country artists such as Joel Crouse, [Brett Eldredge](/page/Brett_Eldredge), [Florida Georgia Line](/page/Florida_Georgia_Line), and [Casey James](/page/Casey_James) on select dates, alongside pop-leaning [Austin Mahone](/page/Austin_Mahone) for U.S. summer shows, allowing Swift to showcase up-and-coming talent aligned with her crossover appeal.[[67]](#ref-67) [Neon Trees](/page/Neon_Trees) supported select international dates, including in [Australia](/page/Australia) and [New Zealand](/page/New_Zealand), bringing [indie rock](/page/Indie_rock) energy to stadium crowds.[[76]](#ref-76) In total, over 10 unique openers rotated across the tour's legs, with announcements made progressively to generate buzz and adapt to local audiences.[[77]](#ref-77)
Special guests elevated the production with surprise duets, often integrated into the set list for spontaneous moments. Ed Sheeran frequently joined Swift onstage for their collaborative track "Everything Has Changed" during North American and European legs, fostering a sense of camaraderie that resonated with fans.[[5]](#ref-5) In Foxborough, Massachusetts, Carly Simon made a memorable appearance to perform "You're So Vain," bridging generational pop icons.[[78]](#ref-78) The Los Angeles shows featured multiple cameos, including Jennifer Lopez for a rendition of "Jenny from the Block," Tegan and Sara for tracks from their album Heartthrob, and Sara Bareilles alongside Cher Lloyd for harmonious pop medleys.[[79]](#ref-79)[[80]](#ref-80)[[81]](#ref-81) Other highlights included Neon Trees' Tyler Glenn on "Everybody Talks" in Newark and Nelly for "Hey Porsche" in St. Louis, adding variety and star power to the evenings.[[82]](#ref-82)
These performers were selected for their stylistic [synergy](/page/Synergy) with Swift's Red-era material, emphasizing emotional storytelling and high-energy anthems, while their sets primed audiences for the main production's theatrical entrance.[[83]](#ref-83) Guest appearances, often unannounced until the moment, heightened excitement and occasionally wove into [set list](/page/Set_list) variations for unique show experiences.

### Cancellations and Incidents

The Red Tour experienced one official cancellation during its run. The scheduled performance in [Bangkok](/page/Bangkok), [Thailand](/page/Thailand), on June 9, 2014, was canceled due to political unrest following a military coup in the country.[[84]](#ref-84) Swift announced the decision via [Twitter](/page/Twitter), expressing her disappointment and apologizing to fans, stating, "I am so sorry to everyone who was planning to come to the show. I love you with all my heart."[[85]](#ref-85) In response, the tour added a second show in [Singapore](/page/Singapore) on June 9, 2014, with priority ticket access given to those affected by the Bangkok cancellation to mitigate the impact.[[86]](#ref-86)
Several minor disruptions occurred due to weather conditions at outdoor venues. On July 20, 2013, the second night at [Lincoln Financial Field](/page/Lincoln_Financial_Field) in [Philadelphia](/page/Philadelphia) was delayed by approximately 1 hour and 45 minutes because of [lightning](/page/Lightning) and [heavy rain](/page/Heavy_Rain), prompting the evacuation of over 50,000 fans to the stadium concourse for safety.[[87]](#ref-87) The show proceeded once the storm passed, allowing Swift to complete the full performance without further interruption.[[88]](#ref-88)
Swift encountered a personal health incident during the tour when she accidentally chipped her front tooth on July 6, 2013, while performing at Consol Energy Center in [Pittsburgh](/page/Pittsburgh). The mishap occurred when she swung her microphone stand enthusiastically during a song and struck herself in the mouth, described by Swift as an inadvertent "[uppercut](/page/Uppercut)."[[89]](#ref-89) She continued the show despite the injury and later sought dental treatment, but no performances were postponed as a result.[[90]](#ref-90)
To manage the physical demands of the 86-show tour spanning over a year, Swift's team incorporated scheduled off-days for rest and recovery, including vocal preservation amid the rigorous schedule of back-to-back stadium performances. No major injuries to Swift or her crew were reported, though the tour's intensity highlighted the need for such precautions.[[91]](#ref-91)
Fan-related incidents were limited but notable for their potential safety risks. During the February 1, 2014, show at [The O2 Arena](/page/The_O2_Arena) in [London](/page/London), a male fan rushed the stage during the encore, approaching Swift closely before being swiftly removed by security; she handled the moment calmly, shaking his hand before continuing.[[92]](#ref-92) Reports from various venues noted occasional crowd density issues in high-attendance stadiums, but no severe crowd crushes or injuries among attendees were documented. Swift's production team emphasized enhanced security protocols throughout the tour to address such occurrences and maintain fan safety.[[93]](#ref-93)
Overall, disruptions were resolved efficiently through rescheduling where feasible and direct communication on social media, helping to preserve fan loyalty despite the challenges.

## Legacy

### Cultural and Artistic Impact

The Red Tour marked a pivotal moment in Taylor Swift's artistic evolution, solidifying her transition from country roots to mainstream pop while bridging genres through its setlist and visuals. The production incorporated elements from her Nashville heritage, such as a 45-minute acoustic set featuring tracks like "Mean" and "Our Song," alongside pop anthems including "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together" and dubstep-infused renditions of "I Knew You Were Trouble," demonstrating a deliberate fusion that showcased her vocal range and thematic depth on themes of heartbreak and growth.[[91]](#ref-91) This genre-blending approach, with visuals like a symbolic "house" set piece evoking young adulthood, influenced her subsequent 1989 World Tour by establishing scalable arena storytelling that emphasized emotional intimacy amid spectacle, paving the way for her full pop immersion.[[56]](#ref-56)
The tour significantly bolstered the Swiftie fan community by emphasizing personal narratives and interactive elements, fostering a sense of shared vulnerability that inspired widespread fan engagement. Swift's onstage monologues, often detailing the inspirations behind songs like "All Too Well," created intimate connections in stadium settings, encouraging fans to create and share art, costumes, and stories on emerging platforms like [Instagram](/page/Instagram) and [Tumblr](/page/Tumblr) during 2013-2014.[[94]](#ref-94) This authenticity strengthened communal bonds, with fans adopting red-themed attire and exchanging mementos, laying groundwork for the devoted online networks that define Swiftie culture today.[[91]](#ref-91)
On a broader artistic level, the Red Tour exemplified the scalability of narrative-driven performances in large venues, drawing comparisons to icons like [Madonna](/page/Madonna) for its bold production and cultural resonance. Retrospective analyses since 2020 have credited the tour with empowering female solo acts by highlighting Swift's command of [multimedia](/page/Multimedia) spectacles and [confessional](/page/Confessional) songwriting.[[95]](#ref-95) Its innovative staging, including catwalks that brought Swift closer to audiences of up to 60,000, set a benchmark for female performers navigating genre shifts under public gaze.[[91]](#ref-91) The tour's associated [album](/page/Album) Red received a Grammy Award nomination for Album of the Year in 2013, further affirming its role in Swift's critical acclaim.[[96]](#ref-96)
The tour also generated significant media discourse on themes of young adulthood, with 2013-2014 think pieces examining Swift's maturation amid intense scrutiny over her relationships and public image. Publications analyzed how tracks and visuals addressed emotional turbulence, positioning Swift as a voice for navigating fame's pressures, as seen in coverage of her evolving persona from "twangy teen" to pop innovator.[[97]](#ref-97) This coverage underscored the tour's role in reframing narratives of female celebrity, emphasizing resilience and self-definition.[[56]](#ref-56)

### Long-Term Commercial Influence

The Red Tour established key precedents for [country](/page/Country)-pop hybrid tours by showcasing a scalable production model that blended intimate [country storytelling](/page/Storytelling) with pop spectacle in [stadium](/page/Stadium) settings, paving the way for similar grossing strategies among subsequent artists. Carrie Underwood's Cry Pretty Tour (2019), which grossed $46.8 million across 55 dates, adopted comparable high-production elements and fan-engagement tactics inspired by Swift's approach to maximizing revenue through merchandise and secondary markets.[[98]](#ref-98)
In ticketing, the Red Tour accelerated the adoption of [fan club](/page/Fan_club) presales via her official website, allowing priority access for members and reducing initial [scalping](/page/Scalping) exposure, a model that evolved into broader anti-[scalping](/page/Scalping) technologies like Verified Fan and remains a standard in 2025 tour planning for major artists to ensure fair distribution.[[99]](#ref-99)
Retrospective rankings affirm the tour's sustained value, with [Billboard](/page/Billboard) including it in its 2020 update to the "top tours of the [2010s](/page/2010s)" as the decade's highest-grossing country outing at $150.2 million, and inflation-adjusted analyses in subsequent years underscoring its benchmark status for genre-crossing profitability.[[100]](#ref-100)[[2]](#ref-2)

The Reputation Stadium Tour was the fifth headlining [concert tour](/page/Concert_tour) by American [singer-songwriter](/page/Singer-songwriter) [Taylor Swift](/page/Taylor_Swift), and her first to exclusively play stadium venues, launched to promote her sixth studio album, [Reputation](/page/Reputation) (2017).[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2)
The tour consisted of 53 shows across seven countries—[United States](/page/United_States), [Canada](/page/Canada), [United Kingdom](/page/United_Kingdom), [Ireland](/page/Ireland), [Australia](/page/Australia), [New Zealand](/page/New_Zealand), and [Japan](/page/Japan)—beginning on May 8, 2018, at [University of Phoenix](/page/University_of_Phoenix) Stadium in [Glendale, Arizona](/page/Glendale,_Arizona), and ending on November 21, 2018, at [Tokyo Dome](/page/Tokyo_Dome) in [Tokyo](/page/Tokyo), [Japan](/page/Japan).[[3]](#ref-3)[[4]](#ref-4) Featuring elaborate production elements including a snake-inspired stage design, massive LED screens, hydraulic platforms, and fireworks, the shows typically lasted nearly two hours and included a mix of [Reputation](/page/Reputation) tracks alongside hits from Swift's earlier albums, with nightly acoustic "surprise songs" performed on secondary stages.[[1]](#ref-1)[[2]](#ref-2)[[5]](#ref-5)
Opening acts varied by leg, with [Camila Cabello](/page/Camila_Cabello) and [Charli XCX](/page/Charli_XCX) supporting the North American and European dates, while [Broods](/page/Broods) joined for the [Oceania](/page/Oceania) shows.[[6]](#ref-6) The tour was a commercial juggernaut, grossing $345.7 million from 2.9 million tickets sold, marking it as the highest-grossing U.S. tour in boxscore history at the time and Swift's biggest earner until her [Eras Tour](/page/The_Eras_Tour).[[7]](#ref-7)[[8]](#ref-8)[[9]](#ref-9)
Critics praised the tour for its high-energy spectacle, Swift's vocal prowess, and thematic cohesion tying into Reputation's narrative of resilience and reinvention, with reviews hailing it as the peak of her live performances and one of the best tours of 2018.[[10]](#ref-10)[[1]](#ref-1) Notable moments included surprise guest appearances by artists like [Maren Morris](/page/Maren_Morris), [Tim McGraw](/page/Tim_McGraw), and [Faith Hill](/page/Faith_Hill), as well as Swift's philanthropic efforts, including inviting 2,000 foster and adopted children to a pre-tour rehearsal concert in [Arizona](/page/Arizona) for free.[[11]](#ref-11)[[12]](#ref-12)[[13]](#ref-13)
The tour's Dallas show on October 6, 2018, was documented in the Netflix concert film Taylor Swift: Reputation Stadium Tour, directed by Paul Dugdale, which premiered on December 31, 2018, and highlighted behind-the-scenes preparations alongside full performances, earning acclaim for its intimate portrayal of Swift's artistry amid intense media scrutiny. The film was later made available for purchase and rental on various platforms after leaving Netflix in 2023.[[14]](#ref-14)[[15]](#ref-15)[[16]](#ref-16)

## Background and development

### Announcement and promotion

Taylor Swift announced the Reputation Stadium Tour on November 13, 2017, via her official website and social media channels, shortly after the release of her sixth studio album, Reputation, on November 10, 2017.[[17]](#ref-17) The initial reveal detailed the first leg of 27 stadium shows across North America, set to commence on May 8, 2018, at University of Phoenix Stadium in Glendale, Arizona, and conclude on October 6, 2018, at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas.[[18]](#ref-18) This tour marked Swift's first all-stadium production and was explicitly positioned in support of Reputation, an album exploring themes of intense media scrutiny on her personal life and personal empowerment amid public backlash.[[19]](#ref-19)
Promotional efforts for the tour were deeply integrated with the album's marketing campaign, which had begun earlier in 2017 with a deliberate [social media](/page/Social_media) blackout across Swift's platforms in late August, followed by cryptic teasers such as timestamped videos and newspaper-style advertisements hinting at reclaiming her [narrative](/page/Narrative).[[20]](#ref-20) Key singles like "...Ready for It?", released as a promotional track on September 3, 2017, and sent to radio on October 24, 2017, built anticipation by showcasing the album's bold, trap-influenced sound that aligned with the tour's high-energy [stadium](/page/Stadium) format.[[21]](#ref-21) Exclusive merchandise lines, including apparel and accessories themed around Reputation's snake motif and dark aesthetic, were launched alongside the [album](/page/Album) and extended into tour-specific items available through presales, further immersing fans in the album's [narrative](/page/Narrative) of resilience.[[22]](#ref-22)
To facilitate fan access, Swift implemented the Taylor Swift Tix program, a verified fan system where participants earned "boosts" toward presale eligibility by engaging with her [music](/page/Music), such as purchasing [Reputation](/page/Reputation) or streaming videos, rewarding dedicated supporters with priority entry starting December 5, 2017.[[23]](#ref-23) General ticket sales opened on December 13, 2017, via [Ticketmaster](/page/Ticketmaster), with subsequent announcements adding European dates in December 2017, [Oceania](/page/Oceania) leg in May 2018, and Japan dates in August 2018, the tour ultimately expanding to 53 shows across [North America](/page/North_America), [Europe](/page/Europe), [Oceania](/page/Oceania), and [Asia](/page/Asia) to meet demand, emphasizing Swift's strategy of direct fan engagement over traditional media promotion.[[24]](#ref-24)[[25]](#ref-25)

### Production and staging

The production of Taylor Swift's Reputation Stadium Tour was led by show director and lighting designer Baz Halpin, who oversaw the integration of theatrical elements with high-tech visuals to embody the album's themes of media scrutiny and rebirth.[[26]](#ref-26) Associate director Melissa Garcia collaborated closely with Halpin to choreograph transitions between performance segments, while [production designer](/page/Production_designer) Tamlyn Wright crafted the overall aesthetic, incorporating [serpentine](/page/The_Serpentine) motifs drawn from the album's imagery.[[27]](#ref-27) Production manager Arthur Kemish handled logistics for the 53-show run, ensuring seamless execution across continents.[[28]](#ref-28)
Staging innovations centered on a dramatic V-shaped main stage spanning 55 meters wide, with each arm extending 33 meters to create a 66-meter performance area that immersed audiences in the narrative.[[28]](#ref-28) A 172-foot by 40-foot curved LED video wall dominated the backdrop, splitting into 12 movable columns that fragmented into 48 individual screens for dynamic projections of snakes and shadowy figures, enhancing the tour's cinematic feel.[[27]](#ref-27) The snake-like catwalk snaked through the crowd via two B-stages, allowing Swift to interact intimately, while a 30-foot inflatable cobra prop rose behind the stage during key moments, accompanied by thematic elements like a giant snake basket for dramatic entrances.[[28]](#ref-28) Confetti cannons and pyrotechnics punctuated high-energy sequences, with two flying gondolas enabling aerial movements that symbolized escape and empowerment.[[27]](#ref-27)
Rehearsals took place over four weeks at Rock Lititz in [Pennsylvania](/page/Pennsylvania), where the team constructed a partial setup due to venue height constraints, focusing on synchronizing the video mag deck—featuring shifting LED panels—with live [choreography](/page/Choreography) and lighting cues programmed by associate lighting designer Eric Marchwinski.[[28]](#ref-28) This process refined the tour's technical precision, including zip-line flights from front-of-house towers and the integration of a custom PA system hung on six 13-meter cantilevers for optimal sound distribution.[[26]](#ref-26)
Logistically, the production required four modular steel systems for the stage framework, each transported via 19 semi-trucks, totaling over 70 trucks alongside additional rigs for video, lighting, and [audio equipment](/page/Audio_equipment).[[28]](#ref-28) Safety protocols adhered to standard stadium-scale standards, including walk-through metal detectors for all attendees, venue-specific clear bag policies (e.g., A4 size in [Australia](/page/Australia), 12” x 6” x 12” in the [US](/page/United_States)), and prohibitions on professional cameras and large signs to mitigate risks in crowds exceeding 50,000.[[29]](#ref-29)[[30]](#ref-30) These measures, combined with on-site medical teams and evacuation plans, ensured secure operations throughout the international itinerary.[[30]](#ref-30)

## Set list and performances

### Standard set list

The standard [set list](/page/Set_list) for the Reputation Stadium Tour was structured to mirror the narrative arc of Taylor Swift's sixth studio album, [Reputation](/page/Reputation), progressing from themes of media scrutiny and defiance in the opening tracks to [vulnerability](/page/Vulnerability) and triumphant reclamation in the later sections, while incorporating select [hits](/page/Hits_+) from earlier albums to underscore her career evolution. This sequence emphasized 10 fixed tracks from [Reputation](/page/Reputation), with additional ones appearing in surprise segments, blending high-production numbers with intimate acoustic moments for dynamic pacing. The [set list](/page/Set_list) remained largely consistent across the 53-show run, with the fixed backbone providing a thematic journey from aggressive anthems to reflective ballads and celebratory closers.[[31]](#ref-31)
The full main set list, as performed on opening night in [Glendale, Arizona](/page/Glendale,_Arizona) (representative of the standard order, excluding one-off guest appearances), was as follows:

- "...Ready for It?"

- "[I Did Something Bad](/page/I_Did_Something_Bad)"

- "Gorgeous"

- "Style / Love Story / [You Belong with Me](/page/You_Belong_with_Me)" (medley)

- "[Look What You Made Me](/page/Look_What_You_Made_Me) Do"

- "End Game"

- "King of My Heart"

- "Delicate"

- "[Shake It Off](/page/Shake_It_Off)" (acoustic)

- "Dancing with Our Hands Tied" (acoustic)

- "[All Too Well](/page/All_Too_Well)" (acoustic)

- "[Blank Space](/page/Blank_Space)"

- "Dress"

- "Bad Blood / [Should've Said No](/page/Should)" (medley)

- "Don't Blame Me"

- "Long Live / [New Year's Day](/page/New_Year)" (medley, piano)

- "...Ready for It?" (reprise)

- "[Shake It Off](/page/Shake_It_Off)"

Subsequent shows featured variations in the acoustic segment (positions 9–11), where Swift performed a surprise song instead of fixed repeats like "Shake It Off," but the overall structure and remaining tracks stayed consistent to maintain the album's storytelling flow. The surprise song was a single acoustic performance on guitar or [piano](/page/Piano) during the b-stage, replacing the fixed acoustic tracks from opening night.[[2]](#ref-2)[[31]](#ref-31)
Performances were characterized by high-energy choreography involving 16 dancers in synchronized routines, particularly during Reputation-heavy segments like "[I Did Something Bad](/page/I_Did_Something_Bad)" and "Look What You Made Me Do," which incorporated snake-inspired visuals and [pyrotechnics](/page/Pyrotechnics) to evoke the album's motifs of rebirth and resilience. Swift underwent eight costume changes designed by [Jessica Jones](/page/Jessica_Jones), featuring glittering bodysuits, flowing gowns, and metallic ensembles in black, gold, and purple tones that aligned with the tour's dark, glamorous aesthetic—such as the sparkling black [jumpsuit](/page/Jumpsuit) for the opening act and the pink "cotton candy" [dress](/page/Dress) for acoustic interludes. Transitions between acts utilized massive LED screens displaying scrolling "news ticker" headlines mimicking tabloid gossip about Swift, reinforcing the [reputation](/page/Reputation) theme before seamlessly shifting to the next song via stage elevators and hydraulic platforms.[[32]](#ref-32)[[33]](#ref-33)[[34]](#ref-34)[[35]](#ref-35)
The set list evolved during pre-tour rehearsals in April 2018, where Swift and her team made final tweaks to song order and transitions for optimal pacing, ensuring the concert clocked in at approximately two hours while balancing high-production spectacle with emotional depth.[[36]](#ref-36)[[37]](#ref-37)

### Surprise songs and variations

The surprise songs segment of the Reputation Stadium Tour featured an acoustic encore where [Taylor Swift](/page/Taylor_Swift) performed one unique song per show, typically on [guitar](/page/Guitar) or [piano](/page/Piano) during the b-stage portion of the [concert](/page/Concert). This intimate interlude provided a stark contrast to the tour's high-production Reputation-focused setlist, emphasizing stripped-down renditions of rarities and deep cuts from her earlier discography to foster a personal connection with fans.[[5]](#ref-5)[[38]](#ref-38)
Across the tour's 53 dates from May to November 2018, Swift delivered 46 distinct surprise songs, with select tracks repeated at multiple venues to accommodate the schedule while maintaining variety.[[39]](#ref-39)[[40]](#ref-40) Notable examples included "All Too Well" from Red, performed in Glendale, Pasadena, and Arlington; "Wildest Dreams" from 1989 in Santa Clara; and "Holy Ground" from Red in Seattle.[[41]](#ref-41) Other rarities encompassed "Teardrops on My Guitar" from her debut album in East Rutherford and "The Best Day" from Fearless in Foxborough, highlighting her willingness to revisit pre-Reputation material.[[42]](#ref-42)
Selections often drew from fan favorites across eras like [1989](/page/1989), [Red](/page/Red), and [Speak Now](/page/Speak_Now), with variations such as mashups—including "Dancing with Our Hands Tied" blended with elements from other tracks in some performances—to add spontaneity and emotional depth.[[5]](#ref-5) This approach showcased the breadth of Swift's catalog, turning each show's acoustic moment into a highlight that rewarded dedicated attendees with exclusive live interpretations rarely heard in full-production settings.[[38]](#ref-38)

### Special guests

Throughout the Reputation Stadium Tour, Taylor Swift invited a variety of special guests to join her onstage for duets during the acoustic segment, creating collaborative highlights that amplified the tour's themes of camaraderie and defiance against public scrutiny. These appearances typically featured renditions of the guests' signature songs, selected for their energetic appeal and personal significance to Swift, and occurred on approximately 10 dates across the North American and European legs. The guests, often close friends or respected peers in pop and [country music](/page/Country_music), were chosen based on longstanding professional and personal connections, such as shared collaborations or mutual support during Swift's career challenges.[[43]](#ref-43)
Notable performances included Shawn Mendes dueting "There's Nothing Holdin' Me Back" at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California, on May 18, 2018, marking an early tour highlight with the Canadian singer's soaring vocals complementing Swift's.[[43]](#ref-43) The following night, May 19, 2018, at the same venue, Troye Sivan performed "My My My!" and Selena Gomez joined for "Hands to Myself," both longtime friends whose presence underscored themes of loyalty amid Swift's reputational battles.[[43]](#ref-43) In London at Wembley Stadium, Niall Horan sang "Slow Hands" on June 22, 2018, and Robbie Williams delivered "Angels" the next evening, June 23, infusing British flair into the international leg.[[43]](#ref-43) Other key moments featured Hayley Kiyoko on "Curious" at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, on July 26, 2018; Bryan Adams with "Summer of '69" at Rogers Stadium in Toronto on August 4, 2018; and Tim McGraw and Faith Hill revisiting Swift's debut single "Tim McGraw" at Nissan Stadium in Nashville on August 25, 2018, a nod to her country roots.[[44]](#ref-44)[[12]](#ref-12)
The tour's final U.S. shows on October 6, 2018, at [AT&T Stadium](/page/AT&T_Stadium) in [Arlington, Texas](/page/Arlington,_Texas), brought out multiple guests, including [Maren Morris](/page/Maren_Morris) for "The Middle" and [Sugarland](/page/Sugarland) for their co-written track "Babe," the latter making its live debut and emphasizing resilience through artistic partnerships.[[11]](#ref-11)[[45]](#ref-45) These collaborations, rehearsed discreetly to maintain surprise, extended set lists organically and heightened audience engagement by blending Swift's narrative-driven performance with guest artists' hits, often tying into Reputation's motifs of overcoming adversity through alliances.[[46]](#ref-46) In total, around 12 unique artists or groups appeared as special guests, fostering a sense of communal triumph that resonated with fans.[[44]](#ref-44)

## Tour itinerary

### North American leg

The North American leg of the Reputation Stadium Tour comprised 40 stadium concerts across 28 cities in the United States and [Canada](/page/Canada). The leg was split into two parts, spanning from May to early June 2018 and from late June to October 2018, with the European leg in between.[[39]](#ref-39) This portion marked Taylor Swift's first all-stadium outing, emphasizing large-scale production in major venues while navigating a packed schedule with brief interludes for international extensions.[[39]](#ref-39)

All 40 shows sold out, drawing a total attendance of 2,168,706 fans with an average of over 54,000 per night.[[39]](#ref-39) Multi-night runs in key markets underscored the tour's demand, including two shows each at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, [Soldier Field](/page/Soldier_Field) in [Chicago](/page/Chicago), and [AT&T Stadium](/page/AT&T_Stadium) in Arlington, as well as three-night stands at [MetLife Stadium](/page/MetLife_Stadium) in East Rutherford and [Gillette Stadium](/page/Gillette_Stadium) in Foxborough.[[39]](#ref-39)
Regional highlights included sentimental homecoming performances, such as the August 25 concert at Nashville's Nissan Stadium, where Swift celebrated her [Tennessee](/page/Tennessee) origins by joining [Tim McGraw](/page/Tim_McGraw) and [Faith Hill](/page/Faith_Hill) onstage for a rendition of "Tim McGraw."[[12]](#ref-12) Similarly, the July 13–14 dates at Philadelphia's [Lincoln Financial Field](/page/Lincoln_Financial_Field) served as a personal return to her [Pennsylvania](/page/Pennsylvania) roots, with Swift visiting her childhood home in Reading beforehand.[[47]](#ref-47)
Logistically, Swift relied on private jet travel to cover the extensive North American distances efficiently between dates. Fan-organized meetups in host cities fostered pre-show excitement and community among attendees. Weather occasionally influenced performances, such as the rain-soaked shows at [MetLife Stadium](/page/MetLife_Stadium) on July 20–22, where Swift continued without major interruptions despite flash flood warnings.[[48]](#ref-48) The leg's second part concluded in Arlington on October 6, after which the tour proceeded to the [Oceania](/page/Oceania) leg.[[39]](#ref-39)

### European leg

The European leg of the Reputation Stadium Tour followed the initial North American shows, featuring six sold-out stadium shows across the [UK](/page/United_Kingdom) and [Ireland](/page/Ireland) in June 2018. These included two performances each at Etihad Stadium in [Manchester](/page/Manchester) on June 8 and 9, Croke Park in [Dublin](/page/Dublin) on June 15 and 16, and Wembley Stadium in [London](/page/London) on June 22 and 23. The leg drew a total attendance of approximately 353,000 fans, showcasing Swift's global appeal amid the album's themes of media scrutiny and personal reinvention.[[39]](#ref-39)
To suit European audiences, the tour incorporated adjustments such as earlier evening start times—Taylor [Swift](/page/Taylor_Swift) took the stage at 8:15 p.m. at [Wembley](/page/Wembley), aligning with local preferences compared to later North American slots around 8:45 p.m. or later—while maintaining the core staging and setlist integrity. International fan travel was encouraged through bundled ticket and accommodation packages offered via official partners like [Ticketmaster](/page/Ticketmaster), facilitating attendance from across Europe and beyond. Local promotion was amplified by [BBC](/page/BBC) coverage, including news features on the Manchester opener where [Swift](/page/Taylor_Swift) acknowledged the city's resilience post-2017 bombing, and interviews highlighting the tour's cultural impact.[[49]](#ref-49)[[50]](#ref-50)[[51]](#ref-51)
The Wembley shows stood out as the leg's high-profile finale, with back-to-back sell-outs attracting 143,427 attendees and generating over $12 million in revenue. Special guests enhanced the excitement, including [Robbie Williams](/page/Robbie_Williams) joining Swift for renditions of his 1997 hit "Angels" on both nights, a nod to British pop heritage. [Niall Horan](/page/Niall_Horan) performed "Slow Hands" at the London Wembley show on June 22, adding to the collaborative energy. European fans responded enthusiastically to the production's "American" motifs—like snake imagery symbolizing media attacks and references to U.S. [celebrity culture](/page/Celebrity_culture)—interpreting them through a universal lens of personal empowerment, resulting in loud sing-alongs and visible emotional connections during songs like "Look What You Made Me Do."[[39]](#ref-39)[[52]](#ref-52)[[53]](#ref-53)
The leg wrapped with the June 23 Wembley performance, serving as a triumphant close to the European extension before the tour resumed in [North America](/page/North_America). Swift later reflected on this phase in the Netflix concert film reputation Stadium Tour, noting how the overseas crowds' passion helped her reclaim her narrative after years of public challenges, affirming the tour's role in fostering deeper fan bonds worldwide.[[54]](#ref-54)

### Oceania leg

The Oceania leg of the Reputation Stadium Tour featured five sold-out stadium shows in [Australia](/page/Australia) and [New Zealand](/page/New_Zealand) in October and November 2018, supported by [Charli XCX](/page/Charli_XCX) and [Broods](/page/Broods). This leg highlighted Swift's expansion to the region, with performances in major venues drawing enthusiastic crowds.[[8]](#ref-8)

The leg concluded in [Auckland](/page/Auckland) before moving to [Japan](/page/Japan).[[7]](#ref-7)

### Japanese leg

The Japanese leg consisted of two sold-out shows at [Tokyo Dome](/page/Tokyo_Dome) in [Tokyo](/page/Tokyo), [Japan](/page/Japan), on November 20 and 21, 2018, supported by [Charli XCX](/page/Charli_XCX). The performances drew 100,109 attendees, generating significant revenue and closing the tour on a high note with pyrotechnics and full production.[[7]](#ref-7)

## Commercial performance

### Ticket sales and attendance

The ticket sales for Taylor Swift's Reputation Stadium Tour were managed through a presale system via the Taylor Swift Tix portal, where fans registered and earned "boosts" to improve their access priority by purchasing the reputation album, merchandise, or referring friends.[[23]](#ref-23)[[55]](#ref-55) This incentive structure aimed to prioritize dedicated fans, with presale windows running from December 5 to 8, 2017, ahead of the general public onsale on December 13.[[23]](#ref-23)
The general onsale on [Ticketmaster](/page/Ticketmaster) drew significant fan frustration due to high face-value prices ranging from $50 to over $350, the immediate appearance of resale listings despite the Verified Fan system, and the introduction of "Official Platinum" premium seats not available during presale.[[56]](#ref-56)[[57]](#ref-57) While initial sales varied by market—with some shows lingering with available seats—demand ultimately led to all 53 dates selling out, reflecting the tour's strong popularity. [Secondary market](/page/Secondary_market) prices indicated robust aftermarket interest.[[58]](#ref-58)
The tour attracted a total attendance of 2.9 million across its 53 stadium shows, establishing it as one of the decade's major draws.[[59]](#ref-59) Notable peaks included over 118,000 attendees across two nights at the Rose Bowl in [Pasadena, California](/page/Pasadena,_California), and 107,550 at [Levi's Stadium](/page/Levi) in Santa Clara over two performances, both setting venue records for the artist.[[60]](#ref-60)

### Gross revenue and boxscore

The Reputation Stadium Tour generated a total gross revenue of $345.7 million from 53 shows across [North America](/page/North_America), [Europe](/page/Europe), [Oceania](/page/Oceania), and [Asia](/page/Asia), establishing it as the highest-grossing tour by a female artist in history at the time of its completion.[[7]](#ref-7) This financial success reflected strong global demand, with an average per-show gross of approximately $6.5 million.[[7]](#ref-7) In the United States alone, the tour earned $266.1 million from 38 shows and 2,068,399 tickets sold, surpassing the previous record for the highest-grossing U.S. tour held by [the Rolling Stones](/page/The_Rolling_Stones)' [A Bigger Bang Tour](/page/A_Bigger_Bang_Tour) ($245 million from 2005–2007).[[8]](#ref-8)
Key boxscore highlights underscored the tour's economic impact. The opening leg's first seven shows, spanning five cities from May 8 to 25, 2018, grossed $54.1 million with 390,000 attendees, topping Billboard's Hot Tours chart for the week of June 9 and setting venue records at [Levi's Stadium](/page/Levi), [Empower Field at Mile High](/page/Empower_Field_at_Mile_High), and the Rose Bowl.[[60]](#ref-60) The two-night stand at the Rose Bowl in [Pasadena, California](/page/Pasadena,_California) (August 4–5, 2018), generated $16.3 million from 118,084 sold-out tickets, marking the highest-grossing concert event in the venue's history for a single headliner.[[60]](#ref-60) Internationally, the final shows in [Australia](/page/Australia) and [New Zealand](/page/New_Zealand) contributed $30.5 million in the tour's closing quarter, including $14.9 million from two nights at [Tokyo Dome](/page/Tokyo_Dome) on November 20–21.[[7]](#ref-7)
Billboard's quarterly boxscore reports positioned the Reputation Stadium Tour as the top-ranked act on the Hot Tours chart for much of [2018](/page/2018), with cumulative grosses reported in Q2 ($54.1 million from initial shows), Q3 (ongoing North American leg building toward the U.S. record), and Q4 (final international wrap-up).[[60]](#ref-60)[[8]](#ref-8)[[7]](#ref-7) Overall, it ranked as the second highest-grossing [concert tour](/page/Concert_tour) of the year worldwide, trailing only Ed Sheeran's ÷ Tour ($429.4 million).[[61]](#ref-61) The tour's performance also exceeded Swift's prior benchmark, [the 1989 World Tour](/page/The_1989_World_Tour), by 38% in total earnings ($250.7 million from 2015).[[7]](#ref-7)

## Critical reception

### Professional reviews

The Reputation Stadium Tour received widespread acclaim from music critics, who praised its elaborate production and Taylor Swift's commanding stage presence as a triumphant return following her public disputes and hiatus from touring.[[1]](#ref-1) Reviews highlighted the tour's theatrical elements, including massive snake props, pyrotechnics, and dynamic video screens, which created an immersive gothic spectacle that amplified the album's themes of resilience and reinvention.[[62]](#ref-62)[[63]](#ref-63) Swift's vocal delivery was frequently commended for its power and versatility, shifting seamlessly from high-energy anthems like "...Ready for It?" to intimate acoustic renditions that fostered a [sense](/page/Sense) of closeness in stadium settings.[[64]](#ref-64)[[65]](#ref-65)
Critics noted the tour's thematic cohesion, with Swift embodying a fierce, unapologetic persona that contrasted her earlier image while incorporating fan-favorite surprises to maintain engagement.[[63]](#ref-63) Outlets such as [Rolling Stone](/page/Rolling_Stone) described it as Swift's "finest tour yet," emphasizing the innovative staging and her evolution as a live performer who balanced spectacle with personal storytelling.[[1]](#ref-1) Variety lauded the show's blend of "bad blood" aggression and goodwill, pointing to intricate choreography and emotional highs in songs like "Delicate" as highlights of its artistic depth.[[62]](#ref-62) However, some reviewers, including [The New York Times](/page/The_New_York_Times), critiqued challenges in sustaining the "ice queen" aesthetic across the full performance, though these were minor compared to the overall praise for its energy.[[65]](#ref-65)
Billboard positioned the tour as the peak of Swift's career, crediting its record-breaking scale and technical prowess for delivering a near-two-hour spectacle that showcased her growth in blending pop grandeur with intimate moments.[[10]](#ref-10) [NME](/page/NME) focused on the fan service through surprise elements and tributes, calling the UK shows a "terrifically good performance" that reaffirmed Swift's [reputation](/page/Reputation) with humor and absurdity amid the bombast.[[63]](#ref-63) [The Guardian](/page/The_Guardian) echoed this, rating the stadium production a triumph for transforming potentially boilerplate tracks into a preposterous yet exhilarating live experience, bolstered by Swift's solo acoustic interludes.[[64]](#ref-64) The consensus viewed the tour as a bold comeback, revitalizing Swift's artistry through cohesive visuals and unwavering audience connection.[[10]](#ref-10)

### Fan responses

Fans expressed overwhelming enthusiasm for the Reputation Stadium Tour, particularly on [social media](/page/Social_media), where the opening night in [Glendale, Arizona](/page/Glendale,_Arizona), sparked a flood of positive reactions on [Twitter](/page/Twitter). Swifties hailed the production as the "best night ever," with many highlighting the dramatic entrance in a suspended [cage](/page/Cage) and the snake-infused visuals as iconic elements that amplified the tour's edgy aesthetic.[[66]](#ref-66)
The tour fueled extensive online discourse through hashtags like #RepTour, as fans shared clips of surprise acoustic performances during the B-stage segment, including renditions of tracks like "[All Too Well](/page/All_Too_Well)" that elicited strong crowd responses and contributed to the viral spread of fan-captured moments. Positive sentiments often emphasized the emotional intimacy of these encores, where Swift connected directly with audiences, and the Verified Fan presale system, designed to make tickets more accessible to dedicated supporters by limiting access to verified buyers.[[38]](#ref-38)[[67]](#ref-67)
Despite the acclaim, some fans voiced criticisms over logistical hurdles, including extended wait times in the presale queue and inflated [secondary market](/page/Secondary_market) prices that deterred purchases early on, leading to reports of slower initial sales across several dates. These issues were attributed to the high face-value [pricing](/page/Pricing) and the complexities of the ticketing [process](/page/Process), though the tour ultimately achieved widespread sellouts and strong attendance.[[68]](#ref-68)[[69]](#ref-69)
Swifties also engaged deeply with the tour's thematic elements, theorizing that the visuals—such as recurring motifs of darkness and rebirth—mirrored Swift's personal navigation of media scrutiny and relationships, sparking discussions that enhanced the fanbase's interpretive connection to the [Reputation](/page/Reputation) era.[[70]](#ref-70)

## Records and awards

### World records

The Reputation Stadium Tour set several world records in concert touring, particularly in gross revenue and attendance, verified by organizations such as [Guinness World Records](/page/Guinness_World_Records) and [Billboard](/page/Billboard) Boxscore. It became the highest-grossing tour by a female artist in a single year, earning $345,675,146 from 53 shows between May 8 and November 21, 2018.[[71]](#ref-71) This figure surpassed previous benchmarks for female-led tours, including Madonna's [MDNA Tour](/page/The_MDNA_Tour), which grossed $227.4 million globally in 2012. The record stood until Taylor Swift's own [Eras Tour](/page/The_Eras_Tour) exceeded it in 2023.[[71]](#ref-71)
In the United States, the tour established the record for the highest-grossing domestic run by any artist, generating $266.1 million from 38 stadium shows and selling 2,068,399 tickets.[[8]](#ref-8) This outperformed [The Rolling Stones](/page/The_Rolling_Stones)' [A Bigger Bang Tour](/page/A_Bigger_Bang_Tour), which earned $245 million across 27 U.S. dates in 2005–2007.[[8]](#ref-8) The attendance marked the most tickets sold for a U.S. [stadium tour](/page/The_Stadium_Tour) by a solo artist that year, contributing to a total global attendance of 2.89 million across all legs.[[22]](#ref-22) According to Pollstar's year-end data, it was also the highest-grossing North American tour of 2018.
These achievements were tracked through verified boxscore reporting from [Billboard](/page/Billboard) and [Pollstar](/page/Pollstar), emphasizing the tour's scale in stadium venues without relying on arena or smaller formats.[[8]](#ref-8)

### Tour accolades

The Reputation Stadium Tour garnered significant recognition for its commercial dominance and innovative production, underscoring Taylor Swift's successful reentry into stadium performances amid her post-2017 media challenges.
The tour won Tour of the Year at the 2018 [American Music Awards](/page/American_Music_Awards), honoring its status as one of the highest-grossing U.S. tours ever at the time.[[72]](#ref-72) It also secured the [Concert Tour](/page/Concert_tour) of the Year at the 2018 [People's Choice Awards](/page/People), a fan-voted prize celebrating its massive attendance and cultural impact.[[73]](#ref-73)
In 2019, Swift accepted the iHeartRadio Music Award for Tour of the Year, crediting fans for selling over 2 million tickets during the North American leg alone.[[74]](#ref-74) The production further earned Best Pop Tour at the [Pollstar](/page/Pollstar) Awards, acknowledging its elaborate staging and high-energy performances.[[75]](#ref-75)
At the [Billboard](/page/Billboard) Touring Awards, the tour received the Top U.S. Tour honor while being nominated for overall Top Tour. It ranked second on [Billboard](/page/Billboard)'s year-end Top 100 Tours chart for 2018, generating $345.7 million worldwide from 53 shows.[[76]](#ref-76) Additionally, it was nominated for Major Tour of the Year at the 2019 [Pollstar](/page/Pollstar) Awards.[[75]](#ref-75)
